title: The Next Brilliant Career: Netflix Launches Nationwide Search for Australia's Next Great Screenwriter
summary: The program invites emerging women and non-binary writers to apply for a unique mentoring experience in developing their story for screen.
body_text: To celebrate the upcoming release of My Brilliant Career and the legacy of pioneering author Miles Franklin, Netflix ANZ, in partnership with the Australian Writers' Guild and Australia's eight State and Territory Screen Agencies, is today launching 'The Next Brilliant Career'. The initiative invites emerging Australian writers who identify as women or non-binary to submit original, authentically-Australian scripted concepts for the chance to receive invaluable feedback directly from Netflix in developing their story for screen. Following application and eligibility check via the state Screen Agencies dedicated online portals, an independent Australian Writers' Guild panel will shortlist applications. One finalist from each state and territory will then be invited to pitch their concept live at Netflix ANZ headquarters in Sydney in October, and will receive direct feedback from Netflix in developing their story for screen. Eligibility To be eligible, applicants must: Be emerging writers, defined as holding 1-3 reportable writer credits on a commercially released short film, film or television series productions longer than 10 minutes, that has screened at a recognised film festival and/or been supported by a state or federal screen agency Not be a full-time student Be an Australian resident Be aged 18 or over Identify as a woman or non-binary Be available to attend a pitch day in Sydney on 6 October 2026 Submissions Applications open today 4 August 2026 and close 18 August 2026 23.59. Submissions must include scripted stories that are authentically Australian, and include a brief professional biography, working title, logline, intended audience description, genre, an explanation of the work's cultural relevance and personal connection, a one-page synopsis and a five-page writing sample. Writers retain full ownership of their original work throughout the Program. Participation does not transfer any rights in a submitted story to Netflix, the Australian Writers' Guild or any Screen Agency. Selection as a Program participant does not guarantee that Netflix will develop a participant's story, or provide funding or ongoing support beyond the Program. To enter, applicants should head to: If you live in South Australia, you can apply via the South Australian Film Corporation's portal here: safilm.smartygrants.com.au If you live in Canberra, you can apply via Screen Canberra's portal here: screencanberra.smartygrants.com.au/TNBC26 If you live in New South Wales, you can apply via Screen NSW’s portal here: screennsw.smartygrants.com.au/thenextbrilliantcareer If you live in the Northern Territory, you can apply via Screen Territory's portal here: grantsnt.nt.gov.au/ grants/the-next-brilliant- career-2026 If you live in Queensland, you can apply via Screen Queensland's portal here: screenqueensland.smartygrants.com.au/mynextbrilliantcareer If you live in Tasmania, you can apply via Screen Tasmania's portal here: buildingtasmania.smartygrants.com.au/BrilliantCareer If you live in Victoria, you can apply via VicScreen's portal here: my.vicscreen.vic.gov.au/apply-for-funding/ If you live in Western Australia, you can apply via Screenwest's portal here: screenwest.smartygrants.com.au/SWNextBrilliantCareerFY27 The judging process Applications will be assessed on the strength and distinctiveness of the writer's voice, the clarity and compelling nature of the central premise, and whether the narrative demonstrates potential to sustain a series or feature format. Judges will look for a strong command of genre, an awareness of the current screen marketplace, and work that is demonstrably and authentically Australian. Amanda Duthie, Netflix ANZ Content Director said: "Miles Franklin spent her career fighting for the right to tell her own story on her own terms. 'The Next Brilliant Career' is built on that same conviction. Australia has no shortage of extraordinary women writers; we've designed this program to welcome the next generation of bold Australian voices telling stories that resonate here and around the world." Claire Pullen, Executive Director of the Australian Writers' Guild said: "We are proud to partner with Netflix ANZ on 'The Next Brilliant Career.' This valuable initiative aligns with our shared mission to foster diverse talent, champion authentic Australian stories, and create meaningful opportunities for our nation's emerging voices. Together, we look forward to uncovering the next generation of storytellers across Australia." ENDS Additional information: Program terms and conditions: Download here FAQs: These FAQs are a guide to help you understand The Next Brilliant Career initiative before you apply. They don't replace the full Program Terms & Conditions, but help to supplement them. Please read the T&Cs in full before submitting your application. What is The Next Brilliant Career ? The Next Brilliant Career is a development program from Netflix, launched alongside its series My Brilliant Career , in partnership with the Australian Writers' Guild (AWG) and the eight state and territory screen agencies. It's designed for emerging Australian writers who identify as women or non-binary, giving eight participants the opportunity to pitch an original story idea directly to Netflix and receive structured feedback. Who can apply? To be eligible, you must: (i) be 18 years of age or older at the time of application; (ii) be an Australian resident; (iii) identify as a woman or non-binary; and (iv) hold at least one, and no more than three, reportable writer credits on a commercially released short film, film or television series that has screened at a recognised film festival and/or been supported by a state or federal screen agency. Full-time students are not eligible. What counts as a “reportable writer credit”? A writer credit on a commercially released short film, film or television series longer than 10 minutes that has either screened at a recognised film festival, or been supported by a state or federal screen agency. You need between one and three such credits to be eligible: no credits, or more than three, won't meet the criterion. For South Australia only, please note that a “recognised film festival” is defined in the South Australia Film Corporation’s Terms of Trade (see p. 11). When can I apply? Applications opens at 00:01am on 4 August 2026 and close at 11:59pm on 18 August 2026. Late, incomplete or illegible applications won't be considered, so allow enough time to complete every required field before the closing date. How do I apply? Apply through the screen agency for the state or territory where you live: visit the applicable website as hyperlinked below and complete and submit the form by 18 August 2026. Applying through the agency that matches your state or territory of residence is part of the eligibility check, so make sure you're on the right one. Entries must be made to the state in which you currently reside, and to one state only. If you live in South Australia, you can apply via the South Australian Film Corporation's portal here: safilm.smartygrants.com.au If you live in Canberra, you can apply via Screen Canberra's portal here: screencanberra.smartygrants.com.au/TNBC26 If you live in New South Wales, you can apply via Screen NSW’s portal here: screennsw.smartygrants.com.au/thenextbrilliantcareer If you live in the Northern Territory, you can apply via Screen Territory's portal here: grantsnt.nt.gov.au If you live in Queensland, you can apply via Screen Queensland's portal here: screenqueensland.smartygrants.com.au/mynextbrilliantcareer If you live in Tasmania, you can apply via Screen Tasmania's portal here: buildingtasmania.smartygrants.com.au/BrilliantCareer If you live in Victoria, you can apply via VicScreen's portal here: my.vicscreen.vic.gov.au/apply-for-funding/ If you live in Western Australia, you can apply via Screenwest's portal here: screenwest.smartygrants.com.au/SWNextBrilliantCareerFY27 My local screen agency portal isn’t working, how do I apply? If you cannot access your local screen agency portal to apply, please email NextBrilliantCareer@organic-publicity.com. Can I submit more than one application? No. One application is permitted per person, and group applications aren't accepted. What do I need to include in my application? A professional biography (up to 150 words) covering your experience, aspirations and screen industry credits A working title for your story A logline (up to 30 words) A description of your intended audience (one paragraph, up to 200 words) The genre of your story An explanation of the cultural relevance of your story, and your personal connection to it A one-page synopsis of the narrative A screenwriting sample (up to five pages in total) Are there word or page limits I need to stick to? Yes. Your biography should be no more than 150 words, your logline no more than 30 words, and your audience description no more than 200 words. Your synopsis should be one page, and your screenwriting sample five pages in total. These limits help keep the assessment process fair and consistent across every application. What is the assessment process? Your relevant screen agency first checks your application against the program's eligibility requirements. Eligible applications are then reviewed by an independent assessor panel appointed by the AWG, which shortlists up to five applications per state or territory. Netflix reviews each shortlist and selects one participant per state or territory, eight in total, for the program. What is the panel looking for? The Assessor Panel and Netflix assess applications against a consistent set of criteria: (i) a clear and distinct writing voice; (ii) a compelling central premise; (iii) potential for the story to sustain a series or feature format; (iv) understanding of the chosen genre; (v) an authentically Australian sensibility in tone, character or setting; (vi) a clearly identified intended audience; (vii) awareness of where the project sits in the current screen marketplace; and (viii) how the project advances diversity, whether through on-screen representation, themes, narrative or key creatives. When will I know if I've been selected? Selected participants will be notified by phone and/or email on 28 September 2026. If you can't be reached by 5:00pm (AEST) on 30 September 2026, or you decide not to proceed, Netflix reserves the right to select another participant in your place. All participants will be confirmed by 2 October 2026. Will I receive correspondence or feedback if I'm not selected? Given the expected volume of applications, individual correspondence and/or feedback isn't provided to unsuccessful applicants. If you do not hear from us, you have not progressed in the program. What happens if I'm selected as a participant? If you're selected, you'll be contacted by a Netflix representative on 28 September 2026 who will provide further details of the Pitch Day and help to coordinate the transport/accommodation logistics depending on where you live. In advance of the Pitch Day, you will also be asked to provide a high-resolution headshot. Netflix will announce all eight participants nationally and regionally. By submitting your application, you consent to Netflix and its partners publishing your full name and headshot as part of the announcement(s). What does a Program participant receive? Participants are invited to a pitch day with Netflix executives in Sydney on 6 October 2026 (Pitch Day), where they'll present their story directly and receive in-room feedback. Depending on where they live, Netflix will arrange return flights or train travel and up to two nights' accommodation. After the Pitch Day, participants can refine their concept and resubmit it by 6 November 2026, and Netflix will provide final written feedback by 1 December 2026. For the avoidance of doubt, being selected doesn't guarantee that Netflix or its partners will develop your story, or provide funding or ongoing support. What if Netflix is interested in further developing my story? If Netflix is interested in developing your story, discussions and development will proceed through Netflix's usual channels and processes. Who owns the rights to my story? You do. All intellectual property in your submitted work stays with you at all times. Taking part in the Program, including being selected as a participant, doesn't transfer any rights in your work to Netflix, the AWG or any screen agency. Netflix and its partners only have a non-exclusive right to copy, use and distribute your application for the purpose of administering and assessing the Program. How is my personal information used? Netflix and its partners collect and use your personal information to administer and assess the Program. Netflix may also use your details to contact you about future projects and opportunities. title: Innventure's Q2 2026 Earnings: Accelsius Liquid Cooling Momentum Builds
summary: Innventure (NASDAQ: INV) shares Q2 2026 results and doubles down on Accelsius's two-phase liquid cooling for AI infrastructure. See what's next.
body_text: ORLANDO, Fla., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Innventure, Inc. (NASDAQ: INV) (“Innventure”), an industrial growth conglomerate, today announced financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. The company continues to anticipate significant long‑term demand for two‑phase liquid cooling as AI infrastructure requirements accelerate and is focused on executing against the foundational milestones expected to govern scaled market adoption of this technology. These milestones include chip-maker relationships and reference designs, OEM and ODM co-development initiatives, relationships with hyperscalers and the delivery of additional thermal benchmark data. “We firmly believe the industry is moving toward a future where two-phase liquid cooling becomes an essential part of AI infrastructure,” said Bill Haskell, Chief Executive Officer. “While our conviction in Accelsius’ long‑term opportunity has only strengthened, evolving dynamics in the AI infrastructure market, including constraints facing smaller early adopters around power availability, GPU access, and deployment timing, have impacted our near-term expectations and render 2026 revenue generation an imprecise reflection of the meaningful progress Accelsius is making. As a result, we are suspending our previously communicated expectations regarding Accelsius’ 2026 revenue and cash flow targets and shifting our focus to execution against important milestones that govern scaled market adoption, which include forging strong relationships with industry leaders. In light of our expectations regarding Accelsius’ ability to make progress against these milestones and the momentum we are seeing at AeroFlexx and Refinity, we believe Innventure is well positioned to create shareholder value over the long term." Conference Call and Webcast A conference call to discuss these results has been scheduled for 5:00 pm ET today, August 13, 2026. The event will be webcasted live via our investor relations website https://ir.innventure.com/ or via https://innventure-2q26-earnings.open-exchange.net/ . Innventure has posted a slide presentation to accompany the prepared remarks to its investor relations website https://ir.innventure.com/ . About Innventure Innventure, Inc. (NASDAQ: INV), an industrial growth conglomerate, focuses on building companies with billion-dollar valuations by commercializing breakthrough technology solutions. By systematically creating and operating industrial enterprises from the ground up, Innventure participates in early-stage economics and provides industrial operating expertise designed for global scale. Innventure’s approach seeks to uniquely bridge the ”Valley of Death" between corporate innovation and commercialization through its distinctive combination of value-driven multinational partnerships, operational experience, and scaling expertise. Non-GAAP Financial Measures We use certain financial measures that are not calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the U.S. (GAAP) to supplement our consolidated financial statements. These non-GAAP financial measures provide additional information to investors to facilitate comparisons of past and present operating results, identify trends in our underlying operating performance, and offer greater transparency on how we evaluate our business activities. These measures are integral to our processes for budgeting, managing operations, making strategic decisions, and evaluating our performance. Our primary non-GAAP financial measures are EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA. We define EBITDA as net income before interest, income taxes, and depreciation and amortization. Adjusted EBITDA is defined as EBITDA further adjusted to exclude certain non-cash items, non-recurring expenses, and other items that are not indicative of our core operating activities. These may include stock-based compensation, acquisition costs, and other financial items. We believe Adjusted EBITDA is valuable for investors and analysts as it provides additional insight into our operational performance, excluding the impacts of certain financing, investing, and other non-operational activities. This measure helps in comparing our current operating results with prior periods and with those of other companies in our industry. It is also used internally for allocating resources efficiently, assessing the economic outcomes of acquisitions and strategic decisions, and evaluating the performance of our management team. There are limitations to Adjusted EBITDA, including its exclusion of cash expenditures, future requirements for capital expenditures and contractual commitments, and changes in or cash requirements for working capital needs. Adjusted EBITDA also omits significant interest expenses and related cash requirements for interest and payments. While depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, the associated assets will often need to be replaced in the future, and Adjusted EBITDA does not reflect the cash required for such replacements. Additionally, Adjusted EBITDA does not account for income or other taxes or necessary cash tax payments. Investors should use caution when comparing our non-GAAP measure to similar metrics used by other companies, as definitions can vary. Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for GAAP financial measures. In presenting Adjusted EBITDA, we aim to provide investors with an additional tool for assessing the operational performance of our business. It serves as a useful complement to our GAAP results, offering a more comprehensive understanding of our financial health and operational efficiencies. title: Are Expenses Liabilities? How Expenses and Liabilities Overlap
summary: While expenses are the costs of running a business, liabilities record what you owe. Expenses can lead to the creation of liabilities—here’s how.
body_text: You might wonder: Are expenses liabilities? Both expenses and liabilities reflect money moving out of your business, but they represent two different concepts on your financial statements. While expenses are the costs associated with doing business, liabilities are your financial obligations. You might use debt (a liability) to cover an expense. For example, the Federal Reserve’s 2026 Report on Employer Firms shows that 56% of small businesses use external financing to meet daily operating expenses . That borrowing creates a liability. Misunderstanding the difference between liabilities and expenses can result in inaccurate bookkeeping, which could affect your tax filings, strategy, and ability to obtain funding. Learn more about expenses and liabilities, how they affect your balance sheet and income statement, and when an expense turns into a liability—plus, how Shopify tools simplify expense tracking and financial reporting. Are expenses liabilities? No, expenses are not liabilities. They serve different purposes in accounting. Expenses are costs necessary to generate revenue during a designated period. They are the operational outlays listed on the income statement (also known as the profit and loss statement ) for running your day-to-day business, such as buying shipping labels or paying for digital ads. Liabilities are the debts or financial obligations your business owes to external parties in the future, and they appear on the balance sheet . In other words, an expense is what you spent to make money this month. A liability is what your company owes someone else. These distinctions are hard and fast, although a single transaction can sometimes create an expense and a liability simultaneously. For example, when a business buys on credit and doesn’t pay cash immediately, it creates an accounts payable liability. The transaction is recorded as an expense on the profit and loss statement, while the unpaid bill sits in a balance sheet liability account until you pay it. In contrast, paying cash right away for items like office supplies means the transaction is an expense, skipping the liability stage. What is an expense? In accounting, an expense is defined as the economic value consumed or used to help a business generate revenue . Under the accrual accounting method, expenses are recorded when they occur, not necessarily when cash leaves your bank account. Expenses are recorded in temporary accounts that reset to zero at year-end. These entries flow directly into the company’s income statement. Expenses reduce your net income and, if they exceed revenue, can result in net losses. Expenses are classified as operating expenses , which are related to core business activities, and non-operating expenses, which are generally related to the costs of financing or one-off events, like a loss on the sale of an asset. Expenses include: Marketing and advertising. Spending on social media ads and print advertising. Shipping and fulfillment. The cost of packaging materials, third-party logistics (3PL) fees, and postage. Software subscriptions. Monthly fees for your ecommerce platform, accounting software, and email marketing apps. Rent and utilities. The cost of leasing a warehouse for storing inventory or paying for electricity to run your operations. Insurance. Regular payments for product liability or business property protection. Every dollar of expense reduces net income and retained earnings, a component of owner’s equity . If your marketing expenses skyrocket without a matching increase in revenue, your net profit and retained earnings shrink, leaving less capital available to invest in business growth. What is a liability? A liability is a financial obligation or debt that is owed to an outside entity. Unlike expenses, liabilities don’t disappear at the end of the accounting year. They are permanent accounts recorded on the balance sheet , which displays a company’s liabilities, assets, and owner’s equity. Settling a liability usually requires transferring cash, providing goods, or performing services. Managing liabilities effectively ensures your business meets its short-term and long-term commitments. For ecommerce brands, liabilities generally stem from funding inventory, expanding operations, or collecting payments in advance of delivering goods or services. Typical ecommerce examples are: Accounts payable liability. Unpaid invoices from suppliers for manufacturing your inventory. Business credit card balances. Debt outstanding on a card used to buy ad space or supplies. Unearned revenue (or deferred revenue). Money collected from customers for gift cards or product pre-orders where the items haven’t shipped yet. Because you still owe the customer the product, this money is considered a liability until fulfilled. Short-term loans. Funding from alternative lenders to purchase inventory. Current vs. long-term liabilities Accountants divide business liabilities into two major categories based on when repayment is due: Liability type Definition Common examples Current liabilities Financial obligations that your business must settle in one year or a single operating cycle Accounts payable, wages, income taxes owed, and short-term loans Long-term liabilities Debts due in more than 12 months, representing extended financial obligations Long-term debt, including most bonds When do expenses become liabilities? An expense becomes a liability the moment your business incurs a cost but defers the payment to a later date. Under the accrual accounting method, when you purchase a good or service on credit, you must record the expense on your income statement and a corresponding liability on your balance sheet to reflect the required future payments. Let’s look at a common scenario for an online apparel brand. Imagine your store hires a freelance graphic designer to create digital ad assets in late December. The designer finishes the work on December 28 and sends their invoice on January 5. Your terms give you until January 30 to pay. The steps to properly record the transaction are: 1. On December 31, you log the design expense on your quarterly income statement because the work occurred in December. 2. Because you haven’t paid the designer yet, you also log that exact amount under accrued expenses (a current liabilities account) on your December balance sheet. 3. In January, when you pay the invoice, your cash balance drops, and the liability account is cleared. However, both the expense and the liability remain in December’s historical data, showing that the cost was incurred and the debt was owed during that period. This lets you build a profit and loss statement and balance sheet. Are expenses liabilities FAQ Are expenses an asset or a liability? Expenses, which are listed on the income statement, are neither an asset nor a liability, both of which are balance sheet items. Expenses represent the temporary operating costs of running your business for a specific period. Assets represent what your company owns, like cash, fixed assets, inventory, or prepaid expenses. Liabilities represent what your company owes. Is a liability the same as expenses? Liabilities and expenses are not the same. A liability is an unpaid debt or ongoing obligation that remains on your balance sheet until it is paid off or fulfilled. An expense is a cost that occurs during a single accounting period to keep your business running, and it appears only on the income statement. Why aren’t expenses liabilities? Expenses aren’t liabilities because they measure different financial activities. Expenses measure the immediate costs needed to generate revenue today, whereas liabilities measure obligations to make future payments or deliver goods down the line.
